sections.h2: Who sends the Newark property tax bill?
sections.html:
Newark's Department of Finance does both jobs, sending the bill and collecting the money. Essex County gets involved only if an owner contests the assessed value. Two units inside Finance matter to a seller. Assessments decides which real estate is taxable, keeps a map of each parcel and logs changes in ownership and mortgages. Revenue Collections mails the bills, takes payments and chases accounts that fall behind.

Customer service answers questions about a balance Monday through Friday, 9 am to 4 pm, except holidays. The tax lines are 973-733-3791, 973-733-3792, 973-733-3962, 973-733-8098 and 973-733-3978. The Payment Center on the city website takes tax payments by credit card, debit card or electronic check. Sellers should phone before the first showing, so the balance is known long before a contract arrives.

Four installments make up the year, and the dates match the quarterly schedule used all over New Jersey. Interest builds on late amounts, and a big delinquency can draw an extra penalty at year end.

Newark quarterly due dates with the interest ceiling for late payments
InstallmentDue dateHighest interest on a late amount
FirstFebruary 18 percent on the first $1,500 owed, 18 percent on the rest
SecondMay 1Same limits
ThirdAugust 1Same limits
FourthNovember 1Same limits

When the fiscal year closes, a delinquency above $10,000 can also draw a penalty of up to 6 percent.

Newark credits a partial payment to the oldest quarter still open. Suppose an owner is behind three quarters and mails a check in September: it reduces the first quarter's principal and interest, and the later quarters stay unpaid. As a result, the payoff figure on a closing statement may be bigger than a quick add-up of the latest bill would suggest.

sections.h2: What happens to a Newark house when taxes go unpaid?
sections.html:
A tax lien certificate on the house goes up for sale. Newark holds a standard sale for earlier years' taxes and charges still owed, plus an accelerated sale for current-year charges left unpaid after the statutory date of November 10. N.J.S.A. 54:5-19 is the state law behind prior-year balances.

  • Whoever buys the certificate gets a lien, not title to the house.
  • Six months after the sale a town holder may sue to foreclose, while a private holder must wait two years.
  • Before final judgment the owner may demand in writing a sheriff's sale, which protects any equity above the debt.
  • The right to redeem lasts until the Superior Court enters a judgment cutting it off.

Our separate New Jersey tax sale guide goes deeper on redemption costs and how to make the equity demand.

sections.h2: How to appeal your Newark assessment
sections.html:
File Form A-1 with the Essex County Board of Taxation, along with its companion comparable sales form. The board must have the petition in hand by April 1, or by May 1 if Newark has just completed a revaluation or reassessment. A property assessed above $1,000,000 can skip the board and go straight to the State Tax Court.

The owner carries the burden of proof and must show that the assessed value is unreasonable compared with market value. To count as excessive or discriminatory, an assessment has to miss on two tests at once: the true market value standard and the common level range, which runs 15 percent either side of the district's average ratio.

  • After a county board judgment you have 45 days to appeal to the Tax Court of New Jersey.
  • Added or omitted assessments, which follow changes made to a property after October 1, are contested on Form AA-1.
  • An added assessment totaling more than $750,000 may be taken directly to the Tax Court.

Newark is the largest city in New Jersey and the seat of Essex County. The estimate for July 2025 is 323,808 residents on 24.14 square miles of land. Only 24.4 percent of homes are owner-occupied. The middle value of an owned home is $373,700, median gross rent is $1,392, and the city counts 113,384 households with a median income of $52,060.

With so many renters, a seller frequently has tenants in place, and any buyer will ask to read the leases. Newark has five wards. Heavy industrial land around the airport and seaport lies mostly in the East and South wards, while residential blocks cluster in the North, Central and West.

A listing gains from nearby transit. Newark Penn Station serves PATH, NJ Transit and Amtrak, and the Newark Light Rail runs from there to Broad Street Station. About 40.3 percent of Newark households had no car in 2020, so buyers often value a short walk to a train.

Before listing, request a written statement from Revenue Collections that lists each unpaid quarter, accrued interest and any tax sale certificate, calculated to the day of closing. The closing agent pays that balance from the seller's proceeds, and the lien is cleared for the buyer.

  • Write down every open quarter, prior-year balances included, because older amounts may already be in a tax sale.
  • Find out whether a certificate has been sold and recorded, and by whom it is held.
  • Mention a pending assessment appeal to your closing attorney so it is handled with the rest of the closing.
  • Budget for the realty transfer fee that the seller pays when the deed is recorded.

sections.h2: What should you line up before closing?
sections.html:
Begin with the payoff. After Finance issues the written statement, give it to your attorney or title company so the exact figure, interest included, can be wired on closing day. If a certificate was sold, its holder releases the lien once paid, and the buyer gets clean title.

Then collect your papers: the most recent tax bill, any county board notice if you filed an appeal, and the name of each mortgage holder. With tenants in the house, add the leases to the pile.

Selling for cash as-is spares you repairs, showings and a lender's appraisal, yet every tax step above still happens. The balance is still paid from proceeds, and the lien must still be cleared before the deed is handed over. Pinning down the number early is what protects your closing date. Finance answers the phones on weekdays only, so plan the request around those hours.

faqs.q: Who do I call to find out what I owe on a Newark house?
faqs.a: Newark Finance customer service takes calls on weekdays from 9 am to 4 pm. Try 973-733-3791, one of five tax lines, and ask for the figure through your closing date.

faqs.q: By what date must a Newark assessment petition arrive?
faqs.a: April 1, unless a revaluation or reassessment was done, in which case May 1. File Form A-1 with the Essex County Board of Taxation. A property assessed above $1,000,000 may go straight to the Tax Court.

faqs.q: What interest does Newark charge on late taxes?
faqs.a: State law allows interest up to 8 percent on the first $1,500 and up to 18 percent on anything above it. A year-end penalty of up to 6 percent can apply when a delinquency exceeds $10,000.

faqs.q: Does paying part of my bill stop a tax sale?
faqs.a: Only partly. Newark applies it to the oldest quarter first, so that quarter's principal and interest shrink while later quarters stay open. A certificate can still be sold for prior-year taxes that remain unpaid.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Newark house that has a tax sale certificate on it?
faqs.a: Yes. At closing the certificate amount plus interest comes out of the sale price and the holder discharges the lien. Request the payoff in writing from the tax collector so the title company wires the correct amount.
